could you shape this into a clear prompt for the coordinator who will prepare the export from the fictional Elm Harbor community survey? the survey ran in April and May 2025, after residents asked the neighborhood association to gather feedback about access to local food. I need a usable CSV export plan, not a write-up of what residents think and not made-up survey results. The coordinator has the survey form and the records; this request is for guidance on arranging those records. Keep the task about the export itself, since the association will handle any later discussion separately.

The form was offered at the library, the Saturday market, and through a web link in the association’s monthly email. Residents could answer about the closest food option they usually use, how they get there, and whether the hours work for them. The survey covered the four named areas: Harbor Point, Mill Lane, Cedar Court, and North Steps. Keep those names as written, and do not combine them into a larger area. The survey was open to adults who live in Elm Harbor. Some people used paper forms and others submitted online, so the coordinator may see the same response fields arriving through different routes.

Please set out an export that can be opened in a normal spreadsheet program and also imported as a CSV. Each row should represent one submitted response, not one person inferred from several records. Use one column per survey field and include a separate response identifier. The source records have a submission date, area, usual food option, travel method, and an answer about whether the option’s hours work. There is also an optional comment field. Keep the original answer wording for those fields rather than rewriting residents’ answers into cleaner-sounding statements. Don't assume that two similar responses came from the same person.

We need missing and declined answers to stay distinguishable. A blank answer means no response was recorded; “prefer not to say” is an actual selected answer, not a blank. Some paper forms have a field left empty, and some online forms were submitted without completing every question, so treat either route the same when a response field is missing. Don't fill gaps from another answer or guess what someone meant. If a date or other value cannot be read on a paper form, mark that value for checking rather than inventing a replacement. The coordinator can use a brief note to explain any blank-value convention in the export plan.

For the travel field, the printed choices were walking, bicycle, bus, car, and other. If someone wrote in a specific answer under “other,” retain the text as entered and keep the category identifiable as other. The food-option answers may name a grocery store, market, pantry, or another place, and the coordinator should preserve the submitted name instead of deciding whether a place belongs to a particular type. There is no need to add a ranking or calculate distance. Keep the answer about hours as the respondent selected it; the form offered yes, no, and unsure.

I want the plan to show how the coordinator can check that each submitted record appears once and that its fields have not shifted into the wrong columns. Include a short numbered section for the checks, such as comparing the row count with the number of submitted records and checking a sample of paper entries against their source forms. These are checks to describe, not claims that the coordinator has already performed them. Please don't create sample results or imply that the survey reached every resident. It was a voluntary survey, and the request is only about preparing the export.

There are privacy limits. do not publish photos, including photographs of respondents, their homes, or identifiable survey-taking locations. This prohibition is about publication of photos; it does not mean the coordinator must discard a photo that is already part of a private source record. The association may publish neighborhood-level response counts as an ordinary allowed action, but the export plan should keep the raw response records separate from any such public counts. Do not turn that allowance into permission to publish an individual record. No photo should be included in the CSV export.

The optional comments need careful handling because someone could include a name, phone number, or detail that identifies a household. One comment in the source says, “We can answer questions, but please don’t put our front door online.” Keep that quotation exactly as written if you refer to it in the prompt, and treat it as an example of why comments should be reviewed before any public sharing. The export request is not asking for the comments to be rewritten, summarized, or published. Explain how the coordinator should keep the original comment available in the restricted source records while ensuring that the export plan does not expose identifying comment text publicly.

Please mention the expected file contents and a practical file label: ElmHarbor_food_access_survey_2025.csv. The plan should identify the columns, explain the missing-answer distinction, and note that the CSV contains no photos. Include a brief description of how to keep the working export with the association’s survey files, without inventing a storage system or access policy that was not supplied. If a required detail is unavailable from the records, tell the coordinator to flag it for follow-up rather than filling it in.

Use connected, clear paragraphs and headings where useful, with the numbered check section included. Keep the distinction between instructions for preparing the export and findings from the survey obvious. The final paragraph should cover the file label and where it belongs among the association’s survey files; it should not add a conclusion about food access, claim that checks have passed, or recommend a later action. Make the result a prompt the coordinator can follow, rather than preparing the export or answering the survey questions.

Please update the small Python utility below so it can read a plain-text list of reminders and produce a predictable, easy-to-test summary. Treat the supplied function as the starting point, not as a finished implementation. Keep the utility self-contained and suitable for someone who wants to run it from a terminal without installing third-party packages. Return the complete revised module once, followed by a concise explanation of the behavior and a few focused tests. Do not include multiple alternative implementations.

The current utility accepts reminder strings and returns them in their original order. Its existing behavior is intentionally simple, and the new behavior should remain understandable rather than growing into a general task-management application. Preserve the public function name and its existing positional argument. You may add keyword-only options if they make the requested behavior clear, but do not introduce a class, a database, persistent storage, network access, or a command-line framework.

```python
def summarize_reminders(lines, limit=5):
    items = [line.strip() for line in lines if line.strip()]
    return items[:limit]
```

1. Input and normalization

The function should continue to accept an iterable of strings, including a generator, and should not require callers to pass a list. Ignore blank lines after trimming surrounding whitespace. For nonblank entries, trim surrounding whitespace and retain the remaining text as the displayed reminder. Do not alter capitalization or punctuation in the displayed text. If an input element is not a string, raise a `TypeError` that identifies the problem as an invalid reminder entry; do not silently stringify it or skip it. An empty iterable should produce a valid empty summary.

Add optional duplicate removal, disabled by default so existing callers continue to see repeated reminders. When enabled, compare entries without regard to capitalization and without regard to surrounding whitespace, while preserving the first occurrence's spelling and position in the output. Do not reorder reminders alphabetically. Explain how duplicates are identified, especially when the text differs only by capitalization.

2. Limits and ordering

Retain the default maximum of five displayed reminders. Support a limit of zero, which returns no displayed reminders, and reject negative limits with a clear `ValueError`. The limit controls the number of reminders shown after blank entries have been ignored and, when requested, duplicates have been removed. Do not consume more of a lazy input iterable than necessary if the chosen implementation can avoid it without making the code confusing. If the limit's type needs validation, state the behavior explicitly and include a focused test for it.

The result should preserve the input order of the retained reminders. Add a summary count that reports the number of valid, nonblank reminders before truncation, applying duplicate removal first when it is enabled. Keep the displayed list and count together in a small, readable return structure, and describe its fields so a caller can use them without examining the implementation. The count is not the number of reminders displayed when the limit has truncated the list.

3. Text-file use

Provide a small terminal entry point that reads a UTF-8 text file whose path is supplied by the user. Each nonblank line is one reminder; do not interpret commas, tabs, or punctuation as separators. The entry point should print the retained reminders one per line and then print the total count in a clearly labeled final line. If the file cannot be read, show a concise error on standard error and exit unsuccessfully. Avoid printing a traceback for an ordinary missing-file or permission error. Keep the function usable independently of this entry point, and keep file handling out of the core transformation function.

There is no need to add sorting, dates, priorities, editing commands, configuration files, or support for multiple input files. Avoid changing the input file, and do not write output files. If the command-line interface needs a choice about duplicate removal or the limit, make the choice explicit in the help text and use the same defaults as the function. Keep the interface modest enough that a reader can understand it from the module alone.

4. Errors and output

Use built-in Python facilities only. Make errors actionable but short, and avoid claiming that malformed input was repaired. The function's returned summary should be deterministic for the same iterable contents and options. Do not include timestamps, random identifiers, logging, or environment-dependent fields. In the terminal output, handle the empty-file case clearly: print the labeled count as zero, without inventing a reminder or substituting a special placeholder for the empty list.

Include tests that cover ordinary ordered input, blank lines, the default limit, a zero limit, a negative limit, duplicate removal while preserving the first spelling, a non-string entry, an empty iterable, and at least one generator. Add a test for the count when the display limit truncates the result. The tests should assert observable behavior rather than private implementation details, and they should run with the standard library's testing tools. Keep test data small and readable; do not add a large fixture or depend on a particular working directory.

5. Response format

Return one complete Python module in a single code block. It should include the function, the terminal entry point, and the tests in a clear arrangement that can be copied into one file and run. After the code block, briefly explain the returned structure, duplicate behavior, and how to invoke the file from a terminal. Do not provide a partial patch, omit unchanged code needed to run the module, or show the supplied implementation again as a separate alternative.

Mara, who maintains the neighborhood list, said, “I can live with a short summary, but I need the count to tell me how many distinct reminders were considered.” Reflect that expectation in the behavior and explanation without changing the displayed wording of any reminder. The utility is for a volunteer who may use it only once a month, so favor clear names and ordinary control flow over clever abstractions. Keep the code compatible with a current Python 3 release, and state any version assumption only if the implementation genuinely depends on one.

When deciding between extra flexibility and a small dependable tool, choose the latter. The completed module should make the distinction between the reminders considered and those displayed easy to see, while leaving the original function name and default limit recognizable to existing callers. Finish with the brief usage explanation; there is no need for a project plan or a discussion of features outside this request.

input:
Write a fictional newsletter feature for people who currently borrow games from the Cedar Lane Community Centre lending shelf. Address those borrowers directly as neighbors who already know the shelf, rather than writing to the centre’s trustees, possible sponsors, or the general public. The piece should follow one ordinary week when volunteers discover that the shelf has become harder to use, then show how they discuss the problem during their usual Thursday opening. Keep the story grounded in small, observable details; it is not a fundraising appeal or a formal policy announcement.

The shelf stands in the centre’s front room beside a low radiator and a noticeboard crowded with swimming lessons, lost gloves, and piano recital flyers. It began three years ago with twelve donated games and now has about eighty, though the collection changes whenever families move, cupboards are cleared, or a box comes back with pieces missing. The centre is open on weekday afternoons, and volunteers keep a handwritten checkout book in a blue binder. Borrowers may take two games at a time for up to three weeks. The feature should explain these familiar arrangements naturally, without turning into an instruction manual or suggesting that every borrower knows each volunteer personally.

Build the episode around a practical mismatch rather than a dramatic crisis. On Tuesday, volunteer Mara finds that the labels on several boxes no longer match the way the games are stored. A cooperative game with a green lid has been placed in the strategy section, while a family game with a similar-sized box is sitting on the bottom shelf with puzzles. No one knows when the mix-up happened. The checkout book shows that both games were returned the previous Saturday, but it does not record who reshelved them. Mara is not angry, and the story should not imply that a borrower caused the problem deliberately. Let her notice the issue while doing routine shelf work, then mention it to the other volunteers on Thursday.

Include two other volunteers with distinct, modest contributions. Leon usually checks returned pieces against the short lists inside the boxes; he has learned that the printed list for one older game calls a wooden marker a “captain” even though the rule sheet calls it a “leader.” Priya makes simple labels by hand and prefers large lettering that can be read from a seated position. Give each person a natural reason for caring about the shelf, but do not supply elaborate personal histories. Include the exact line, “If the lid tells one story and the binder tells another, we should make the shelf easier to read,” as something Priya says during the conversation. It should sound like a practical comment, not a slogan that everyone repeats.

Let the Thursday discussion take place while the centre’s front room remains in use. A child is waiting for a parent near the noticeboard, someone asks where the spare chairs have gone, and a volunteer pauses to answer the centre’s telephone. These details can interrupt the conversation briefly, but they should not become separate plotlines. The borrowers who use the shelf are the intended readers; keep the tone welcoming and matter-of-fact, without speaking as if every reader has volunteered or attended the meeting. Do not address non-borrowers with a request to donate money, games, or time.

Use the following episode details as anchors, while letting them fit into a readable narrative rather than copying them into a checklist:
1. The blue checkout binder stays at the front desk, and returned games are usually placed on a narrow table until a volunteer checks them.
2. The green-lidded cooperative game is called Harbor Lights. Its box has all the pieces, but its paper label has curled away at one corner.
3. The family game is Orchard Market. Its rule sheet is present, though one folded page makes the setup diagram difficult to see.
4. A borrower has asked whether a game for three people can be borrowed for a household of two, but no one at the meeting knows which game the borrower meant.
5. The centre’s craft group uses the room on Wednesday afternoons, so volunteers cannot leave sorting materials on the table overnight.

The discussion may consider a temporary way to make the two misplaced games easier to find, such as checking the shelf labels and writing clearer descriptions after the Thursday opening. Keep any change under discussion distinct from a decision already made. No volunteer should claim to know who returned or moved either game, and the borrower’s question about playing with two people should remain unanswered unless a specific game is identified. The feature can show people weighing convenience against the limited time they have, but avoid manufacturing a dispute or a neat solution that the supplied details do not support.

Close with information for borrowers that is separate from the shelf-label conversation: the centre will be closed on the coming Monday for a boiler inspection, while the front room is expected to reopen on Tuesday at its usual time. Mention that the checkout binder will remain at the front desk during normal opening hours. End on that practical note or another quiet observation from the room, without adding a summary of the volunteers’ discussion, a claim that the shelf has been fixed, or a request for readers to take action. Keep the prose friendly and specific, and let the small uncertainty about how the games were reshelved remain part of the episode.

i need help making a clean prompt from this for a volunteer who handles our community survey export. We are the Eastbank Neighborhood Council, and the survey was called the Maple Ward Safe Routes and Shared Spaces Survey. It was open from April 3 through May 18, 2025. The council has one spreadsheet exported from the online form and another tab where paper forms were entered. They are supposed to have the same questions, but the two sources have not yet been checked against each other. Ask the volunteer to prepare a shareable CSV and a short field guide from those sources, not to write a report about what residents think. I want a prompt that gives the person enough to do the export carefully without pretending we have already checked the data.

The coordinator's tally says there were 214 submissions: 187 marked complete and 27 marked partial. That is a tally from the coordinator, not a verified count from the spreadsheet, so keep that distinction. The volunteer should compare the files and report any count difference rather than quietly replacing the tally or making it look confirmed. We have not agreed on whether records that look alike are duplicates. If a possible duplicate comes up, keep it for review and describe the issue; don't remove it just because the answers resemble each other. A shared record identifier might help with comparison, but I don't know whether both tabs have one, so the prompt should say to check rather than assume.

The questions covered six areas: crossing safety, street lighting, benches, curb ramps, access to the park, and an open comment. Some questions allowed people to choose more than one answer. Preserve those selections in the CSV in a readable way and explain in the field guide how multiple choices are represented. Don't turn multiple answers into a single inferred preference. Keep a blank answer blank and keep the explicit choice “not sure” as its own answer; those aren't interchangeable. The prompt should ask the volunteer to use the same field names for matching questions from both sources when the wording is the same, and to note any mismatch in wording or missing field instead of guessing which question it corresponds to.

Names and email addresses were optional on the form. There may also be an intersection or block description in responses, which could identify a household when combined with other details.
